description.narrative: Sexual exploitation of children (SEC) is a grave violation of children’s rights and affects millions of children and youth annually, regardless of gender. No region, country or child is immune, though girls, boys and children with other gender identities face differing levels of risk to different manifestations of SEC depending on their intersectional vulnerability factors. It impacts heavily and long lastingly on their physical, emotional and mental well-being. It deprives children and youth of establishing healthy (sexual) relationships and from developing to the best of their potential. The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC and will work in 12 countries in Latin America and South and South East Asia: Bangladesh, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Dominican Republic, Guatemala, India, Indonesia, Laos, Nepal, Philippines and Thailand.

The SUFASEC programme is designed to combat SEC by working towards the following long-term impact: “Children in all of their diversity are better protected from sexual exploitation.” This activity forms part of the SUFASEC programme. The long-term impact will be reached through three interlinking objectives that address different dimensions (social norms, assets/environments, and laws/policies/systems). 1. Children, youth and their communities successfully challenge social norms and harmful practices related to SEC 2. Children and youth have access to and are supported by strengthened assets and protective environments 3. Children and civil society meaningfully participate in holding duty bearers, including government and local authorities, accountable to their obligations towards improved (implementation of) laws, policies, and systems

The different stakeholder groups involved in the SUFASEC programme include: - Children and youth in all their diversity: A child-centred approach: children and youth are the most important stakeholders. When children/youth fall victim to SEC the physical and mental impact can be long lasting. The Alliance adheres to the UN definition of child (0-18 years) and youth (15-24 years) - Caregivers and Communities: Critical stakeholders in the community include parents, caregivers, community leaders, teachers, local Community Based Organisations (CBOs), social workers, and other community members involved in community based child protection mechanisms. - CSOs and CBOs: Local child protection organisations support and implement activities at community level, L&A towards national actors, and provide synergies of interventions. - Local and national governments: formulate, endorse and implement laws and public policies related to SEC Private Sector: Travel and tourism orgs (e.g., large and small, hotels, transport), as well as ICT/ Digital Service Providers have interest to avoid SEC taking place within their value chain, and to avoid having their products and services used to facilitate SEC - International donors, Intergovernmental bodies, INGOs, Multilateral entities55: Targeted audiences and partners for evidence based regional and international lobbying - Dutch Stakeholders: NL Embassies in programme countries, MoFA, MoJ&S, to formalise the network for sustainable cooperation to end SEC and impunity of offenders. The Dutch Public - Media & Journalists: Investigative and reporting outlets in the Programme countries. Media and journalists in the Netherlands.

Children and adults were informed about the #BERSAMAMU helpline of SEJIWA during trainings and awareness raising activities of SUFASEC program. The helpline, through its psychologists, provided counseling services to victims of sexual violence, clients undergoing depression and other mental health concerns. Some clients were referred to community health services for STI testing and other treatment for victims of sexual violence. Clients who wanted to pursue legal action were referred to local legal institutions.

Through the various activities we have conducted, we have consistently promoted our counseling services. Therefore, this year, these services continue to run and are expected to reach even more individuals, especially as we collaborate with new communities and organizations.

title.narrative: Children and youth access comprehensive correct SRHR and SEC information
# of young people (gender non-specified) reached with comprehensive, correct information on sexuality, HIV/AIDS, STIs, pregnancy and contraception

comment.narrative: For consistency reason, we set this baseline value as zero in every implementing country. For more info on baseline results see SUFASEC Baseline Report (published as a document into IATI). Endline results will be done by external consultant at the end of the Programme (in 2026) and will compare results included in the baseline report

Topics covered in the trainings and awareness raising activities include online and offline child protection, sexuality education, overcoming stigma and taboos related to SRHR and gender, positive discipline, access to helpline. The participants are also guided to analyze existing SEC cases and asked to raise possible actions and interventions to address the cases. This is the participatory approach employed by SEJIWA to help stakeholders understand the situation and the possible solutions. Children are also involved in creating media campaigns, allowing them to learn more during the process of co-creation and their outputs like videos allows the to reach other children and adults to inform them about SEC, SRHR, including information about the helpline.
Children and youth participants identified themselves either as male or female.

This year, we have partnered with a community advocating for human rights for the LGBTIQ group. This community consists of individuals ranging from adolescents to young adults aged 15-27. This collaboration marks the first step in engaging with the community and enhancing their knowledge and skills through a comprehensive workshop session focused on OCSEA, SRHR, and early psychological support.

Children and youth aged 14 - 21 years old participated in a Socialization which was a safe space for children to express online and offline child protection concerns in their communities, sexual exploitation of children, sexuality education and gender. The children and youth were involved in co-creating media campaigns that were posted in social media.

This year, we are continuing our campaign and outreach program from the first year focused on OCSEA and SRHR. However, this year we have expanded the knowledge and skills to include additional content on online sexual violence cases with the assistance of artificial intelligence, as well as skills on early psychological support. These efforts to enhance knowledge and skills aim to enable adolescents to update their understanding and abilities in preventing sexual violence in the real world, while also equipping them to support their peers who may experience sexual violence both online and offline.

comment.narrative: For consistency reason, we set this baseline value as zero in every implementing country. For more info on baseline results see SUFASEC Baseline Report (published as a document into IATI). Endline results will be done by external consultant at the end of the Programme (in 2026) and will compare results included in the baseline report.

In the second year, we focused on building networks with government institutions concerning OCSEA and SRHR issues. Regarding the urgency of support services, our efforts in the second year, in collaboration with government agencies, centered on enhancing and sharing best practices related to hotline services (psychological support) offered by both government and non-government organizations. Through this strategy, we plan to continue the L&A process in the third year.

Implementing partner will implement lobby and advocacy activities to push the government to strengthen SEC prevention. This process will entail the implementing partner to gather and analyze latest data on SEC and determine strategic actions to engage the government.

Increased capacities towards SEC Prevention and Response of Partners and stakeholders in the communities will be focused on in years 2 and 3. This will include orienting stakeholders about the law on sexual violence crime which was enacted in 2022.
